alignment.note: ἕνεκεν τούτου / ܡܛܠ ܗܢܐ / Propter hoc — standard causal formula.
ἄνθρωπος / ܓܒܪܐ / homo. The Syriac ܓܒܪܐ (g-b-r) specifically denotes 'man, male,' more precise than the generic Greek ἄνθρωπος and Latin homo, though all function here as the marital subject.

Greek expresses 'his father' analytically with article + noun + possessive pronoun (τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ); Latin uses patrem suum; Syriac ܠܐܒܘܗܝ fuses the object marker, noun, and pronominal suffix into a single morphological word — semantically equivalent but synthetically constructed.
καί / et — the conjunction; in Syriac it is prefixed proclitically to the following word rather than standing as a separate token.

Greek τὴν μητέρα and Latin matrem render 'the mother' as discrete article/noun units, whereas the Syriac ܘܠܐܡܗ packages conjunction, object marker, noun, and possessive suffix ('and his mother') into one synthetic form.
καί / et — coordinating conjunction joining the two clauses; the Syriac conjunction is again proclitically attached to ܢܩܦ.
προσκολληθήσεται / ܢܩܦ / adhærebit — 'will cleave/be joined to,' echoing Gen 2:24.

Greek uses the prepositional phrase πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ and Latin the analytic ad uxorem suam, while Syriac ܠܐܢܬܬܗ compresses preposition, noun, and possessive suffix into a single word; the Syriac and Latin both lack the explicit preposition that Greek marks with πρός in periphrastic form.

The Clementine Vulgate closes the clause with a colon, anticipating the continuation in the following verse; neither the Greek (which ends with a comma) nor the unpunctuated Peshitta token stream marks this break identically.
